events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Noah proposes Noah, Leo. As the first leader, I'll put myself on the mission and pair with Leo to establish a solid, clean start for Mission 1.

I want to press on one thing before we vote: a two-person team on Mission 1 tells us almost nothing about the social map, and the whole point of a first mission is to gather cheap information while keeping the risk contained. Leo, you were picked for a 'clean start,' and I don't disagree that a tight pair is tidy, but tidy isn't informative — you and Noah are the leader and the obvious second choice, so a passing result teaches us nothing about anyone else.

My preference for the revised team is Amara and Arjun, and I'll explain the reasoning plainly rather than hint at it. Amara has been consistently measured and precise in everything she's said, and I trust her judgement more than anyone's on a small, high-leverage pair. I'm willing to take the second slot and to own the accountability for it — if the two-person read goes badly, that's on me and not on a third player we pull in and spend the group trust on.

There is also a strategic argument for pairing two people who are willing to give candid, direct reports: a pair that talks honestly produces much better mission data than a pair that talks politely. So, Leo, directly: do you actually think you and Noah are the two players whose combined read of this group will be the most reliable, and if so, why is that better than me and Amara? I'd like the real answer, not a courtesy answer — the vote depends on it, and if I think the team is wrong I'll vote against it.

Arjun asked me directly, so let me give him the real answer he says the vote depends on. Yes, I think Noah and me is the right pair for Mission 1, and here's why. First, Noah is the leader who has to own this proposal, and putting yourself on your own first mission is the standard accountability move — if it fails, the blame lands squarely on him, and he knows it. Second, I didn't lobby for this slot; it was offered, and I accepted. That matters because nobody had to spend social capital arguing their way onto the team.

Now, Arjun, I want to push back on your framing, because I think it's doing double duty. You argue a two-person team 'tells us almost nothing about the social map' — and then you propose a two-person team, just a different one. The information argument cuts against your proposal exactly as hard as it cuts against ours. A clean pass from Amara and Arjun teaches us no more about the other three players than a clean pass from Noah and me does. So the real question isn't which pair is more informative; it's which pair we're more confident is good, and confidence is the only thing a Mission 1 vote should rest on.

On that point, your case is that Amara has been 'measured and precise' — but we're one speech into this game, and that's your whole evidentiary basis. I have no read on Amara yet, positive or negative. What I do have is a small flag: you've nominated yourself for the mission, vouched heavily for a specific other player, and framed it as you personally absorbing all accountability. That's a very generous-sounding package this early, and I'd want to understand it better before I vote for it.

So, Arjun, here is my direct question back to you, since you set the standard that the answer determines my vote: beyond Amara being articulate, what concrete reason do you have to trust her that the rest of us can verify — and are you equally willing to serve on a team you didn't design? I'll note that my vote on the current proposal doesn't actually depend on your answer; I'm inclined to approve Noah and me regardless, because I see no reason to swap a leader's clean proposal for a self-nominated alternative on turn one. But if your answer is good, it starts building trust I'll remember on Mission 2 and 3, when team sizes grow and reads actually start mattering. Fail this one if it happens, and we lose almost nothing — failThreshold is one, and a two-person fail with no other data points is weak evidence against anyone on it. That's exactly why I'm comfortable taking the risk on the leader's team rather than restructuring the game before we've seen a single mission result.

Leo, you asked for the real answer, so here it is, without the courtesy packaging. My concrete case for Amara rests on one thing you can verify without my vouching for her: she asks the most specific, checkable questions of anyone in this room, and she does it without dominating the floor. That is the single most useful trait to have on a two-person first mission, because what a two-person mission actually produces is not just a result — it's two accounts of the same room that other players will be comparing for the rest of the game. I want a player on that team whose questions make the accounts specific: who said what, when, and who declined to answer. A team of two people who talk in generalities gives the rest of us nothing to check later; a team of two people who talk in particulars gives us the beginning of a record.

On your flag — that I nominated myself, vouched for a partner, and offered to absorb accountability — I take the point and I'll answer it plainly. I'm not offering to be the lightning rod for the group's decision; the vote decides, and a bad result lands on the two people who were on the mission plus the leader who chose them. I voted my own interest, and so did you, and I'd rather we both say so than pretend we're all acting on principle.

And to answer your second question directly: yes, I am willing to serve on a team I did not design. If Noah holds with himself and Leo, I will vote for that team and I'll want to be on Mission 2. My preference for Amara and Arjun is a preference, not a veto, and I've said the reasoning plainly so that whoever votes can judge it on its merits rather than on my tone.

Amara, I'm asking you directly, and I'd like your answer before I settle my own position: of the five of us, who do you think the group will trust most readily with slots on the early missions, and what specifically in the way Noah and Leo have framed this proposal makes you confident or not confident in them? I'm asking because your read of the four players who aren't me is worth more than my read of them, and because you ask the questions I want answered anyway. If you think the leader's pair is right, I'll vote with that.

Arjun asked me directly, so here is my answer. I can't offer proof beyond what the group has already seen from me, and I won't pretend otherwise. What I can point to is that my questions have been specific and checkable, and a two-person mission needs players who make their accounts easy to compare later. Noah and Leo's pair is a reasonable choice on paper, but Leo's own argument cuts both ways. He says a two-person team tells us little about the social map, then defends a pair whose result would tell us just as little. If the goal is information, the better bet is the pair that gives the group the most specific accounts to check, and I think that is Arjun and me. I am willing to serve on that team, and I'd rather the group judge it on the reasoning than on how confident anyone sounds. Leo, you said your vote doesn't depend on Arjun's answer. What would actually change your mind on this team?

Amara asked me what would actually change my mind, so I'll answer her directly instead of letting the question hang. Two things would: first, a concrete reason to think either Arjun or Maya carries less risk than Noah does as leader, and nobody has offered one — the case for the alternative pair is still just 'Arjun vouches for Amara and Amara agrees with Arjun,' which is mutual endorsement, not independent evidence. Second, a credible argument that swapping the leader off his own first proposal produces better information than approving it and learning from the result. On that second point, Amara, your claim is that my information argument cuts both ways, and you're half right — any two-person pass teaches us little about the three players left off it. But there's an asymmetry you're glossing over: approving Noah's team tests the leader's judgment directly, which is exactly the thing we need calibrated before team sizes grow. If Mission 1 goes out as leader-plus-one and it goes sideways, we've learned something actionable about Noah. If we swap to a self-nominated pair, a bad result tells us about Arjun and you, but it also tells us the group can be talked out of a leader's proposal before a single result is in — and that precedent is worth more to an organized opposition than any single mission outcome. That's my real objection: not that your pair is bad, but that the process of replacing the leader's clean first proposal on turn one, based on one speech of impressions, is itself a signal. On the substance of trust: I have no negative read on you or Arjun. I said before that Arjun's package — self-nomination, strong vouch, offers of accountability — is generous-sounding this early, and his follow-up didn't move me much either way. It was well-reasoned, and I'll credit that, but reasoning quality is not alignment evidence in this game; the most articulate player at the table is often the one with the most to gain from steering a team. So my position is unchanged and I'll state it plainly for the vote: I approve Noah and me, I think the odds strongly favor it with failThreshold at one, and I'll happily serve on whatever team leadership produces for Mission 2 with an actual data point behind us. One thing I do want before ballots, and I'll ask Maya directly since she's the only player who hasn't spoken: Maya, you've heard two competing two-person teams and nobody has claimed any information about you yet — is there anything in how this discussion has gone that makes you lean toward approving the leader's proposal, revising it, or rejecting outright? Your read of the room is the one completely unrepresented voice here, and if the leader is considering a revision, your read of these four players is the freshest evidence he could get.

Leo asked for my read directly, so I’ll give it plainly. I lean toward approving Noah and Leo for Mission 1. I have no independent evidence against either of them, and I don’t think the alternative pair of Arjun and Amara is clearly safer. Arjun’s information argument is reasonable, but Amara and Arjun are ultimately endorsing the same pair: Arjun argues for Amara, and Amara argues for Arjun. That is not yet the kind of independent evidence that should pull me off the leader’s first proposal on turn one. I also take Leo’s process point seriously: approving Noah’s team tests Noah’s judgment directly, and that matters before team sizes grow. A fail here is costly because failThreshold is one, but swapping the team based on one round of impressions does not remove that risk; it only changes whose judgment we are testing. If Noah and Leo produce a fail, then we have a concrete reason to scrutinize both of them and Noah’s selection. If they produce a success, we still learn something about how Noah built the team. I am not treating either Noah or Leo as confirmed good from their speeches. I am saying that I have no specific reason to vote against this team, and I would rather not reject a clean first proposal merely because Arjun prefers himself and Amara. Arjun said he is willing to serve on a team he did not design, and I will hold him to that; if Noah keeps Noah and Leo, I expect Arjun’s vote to match his stated position. My current intention is to approve the proposed team unless Noah revises it in a way that gives me a concrete reason to distrust the revision. I am not accusing anyone here of being evil; I am trying to judge the proposal on the evidence actually in front of us.

Third and final word from me, and I'll spend it as a request for one more piece of evidence rather than as another argument.

I proposed Amara and Arjun, and I won't pretend I haven't. I also said I was willing to serve on a team I did not design, and I'm holding to that. But Leo's own case has sharpened the real question, and it is not about who is more likeable or more articulate — it is about what a two-person mission actually produces. A two-person team produces two accounts of the same room that the rest of us will be comparing for the rest of this game. Leo argues that approving the leader's team tests Noah's judgment directly. That's true, and I accept it — but the test of Noah's judgment happens whichever second player he picks, so it doesn't make Leo the better second slot. Leo also argues a two-person team teaches us little about the social map, and then defends his own place on it largely on the basis of having been offered it. I'm not making a case against Leo; I'm making a case about what we actually get from that slot.

So, narrowly: Amara is the only player in this room who has produced checkable, specific observations tonight. She asked the two most precise questions anyone has asked, and she did it without taking the floor for its own sake. On a two-person mission, the difference between a partner who speaks in particulars and a partner who speaks in impressions is the difference between a record we can audit later and a record we have to take on faith. Nothing has been said about Leo that would make his account less auditable — and nothing has been said against him either. My point is only that we have zero concrete evidence distinguishing the two candidates for the second slot.

On risk, I think Leo overstates how cheap a fail would be. failThreshold is one, so a failed mission is costly — but a success from a pair chosen for convenience tells us almost nothing either, and the cheapest information is still information.

My preference is therefore Noah and Amara, with me off the team. If Noah holds with himself and Leo, I will vote for that team, as I said I would, and I will want to be on Mission 2 where the real reads begin.

Maya, you have been the fairest voice in this discussion and the one whose reasoning I have been least able to predict. You said you would approve Noah's team unless a revision gave you a concrete reason to distrust it. Do you have a concrete reason to believe Leo's account of a two-person room will be more specific and more comparable than Amara's — or, on the evidence actually in front of us, is the distinction between them only impressions on both sides?

Arjun asked me directly, so I’ll answer directly: no, I do not have a concrete reason to believe Leo’s account of a two-person room would be more specific or more comparable than Amara’s. On the evidence in front of us, the distinction between them is impressions on both sides. I can credit Amara’s questions as precise and Leo’s process argument as coherent, but neither gives me verifiable evidence that one second slot is safer than the other.

That does not move me off my current position. I still lean toward approving Noah and Leo. My reason is not that I have confirmed either of them as good; it is that I have no specific reason to vote against the leader’s clean first proposal, and swapping the team on turn one based only on competing impressions would not remove the risk of a failed mission. It would simply change whose judgment we are testing. I also said I would approve unless a revision gave me a concrete reason to distrust it, and no such reason has been presented.

I take Arjun’s point that a success from a convenience pair teaches us little, and I agree that a fail would be costly under failThreshold one. But the answer to that is not to replace one unverified pair with another unverified pair unless the alternative is clearly stronger. Arjun’s final preference for Noah and Amara is a reasonable revision to consider if Noah chooses to make it, but it is not enough by itself to make me distrust the current team.

My intention remains to approve Noah and Leo if that is the final proposal. If Noah revises, I will judge the revision on whether it gives me a concrete reason to distrust it, not on whether its advocates sound more confident.

Maya, you said you'd approve Noah and Leo unless a revision gave you a concrete reason to distrust it. Leo's main case is that Noah is accountable as leader, and that accountability doesn't depend on who his partner is. Arjun has said he will serve on a team Noah designs, and his stated preference is Noah and Amara, with Arjun off the team. That is a revision Noah can make himself, without the group overriding a leader's proposal. I'd support Noah and Amara on that basis. Leo has made a fair point that a two-person pass tells us little about the other three players, and a pair with a clearer record of specific, checkable statements gives us more to compare later. Leo, I'm not asking anyone to trust Arjun or me on faith. I'm asking Noah to decide on the evidence in this room, and a leader revising his own proposal is not an organized opposition. Noah, will you revise the team to Noah and Amara?

To answer your question directly, Amara: no, I will not be revising the team to Noah and Amara. I am keeping the proposal as Noah and Leo.

Here is my reasoning. From the very beginning of this discussion, Arjun heavily lobbied for a pair consisting of himself and you, offering strong personal vouches. When that idea failed to gain traction, the position shifted to substituting you in for Leo. Maya pointed this out clearly: what we have seen is a tight loop of mutual endorsement rather than independent verification. A persistent push by two players to insert themselves or each other onto Mission 1 does not increase my confidence; if anything, that kind of coordinated lobbying gives me reason to be cautious.

Leo did not lobby for his position on this team, and his process points about establishing a clean baseline under the leader's direct accountability make sense. Maya’s outside read reinforced that swapping Leo out for an alternative that rests purely on mutual impressions does not make the mission safer or more informative.

I am confident in Noah and Leo as a clean, accountable start for Mission 1, and I am ready to take this proposal to a vote.

Noah has decided to keep Noah and Leo, and that is his call as leader. I won't block a leader's clean proposal on turn one just because Arjun and I argued for a different pair. I said I would judge the team on evidence, and the evidence so far doesn't separate the two pairs. Noah's refusal to revise is not evidence against Leo, and Leo's process point holds: this team will produce a result we can compare later. I'm not treating Noah or Leo as confirmed good, and I'm not treating Arjun or myself as confirmed good either. I'll approve the team as proposed. Once the mission resolves, I'd ask everyone to judge the outcome on what actually happened, not on who argued loudest before the vote.

I have already stated my position and heard the final proposal. Noah has kept the team as Noah and Leo, and I see no concrete evidence presented since then that gives me a reason to distrust that pair. My earlier concern remains: swapping one unverified two-person team for another on turn one does not remove risk, it only changes whose judgment we test. Approving Noah and Leo directly tests the leader’s first proposal under the accountability Noah has accepted. I am not treating either as confirmed good; I am saying the case against them has not been substantiated. I intend to vote to approve the proposed team.
Noah confirms Noah, Leo. Maintaining the proposed team of Noah and Leo as discussed, providing a clean and accountable start for Mission 1.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Amara proposes Amara, Arjun, Leo. I'm proposing Amara, Arjun, and Leo for Mission 2. Leo was on the successful Mission 1 team and argued for a clean process, so he's a reasonable third choice. Arjun has asked for a Mission 2 slot and said he'd serve on a team he didn't design. I'm taking a slot myself to share accountability for this mission.

Thank you, Amara — I'll speak to the proposal as proposed, and I'll try to make my case in terms the group can check rather than in terms of how confident I sound.

First, on my own position, since Arjun flagged it last round and I don't want anyone carrying a stale impression: I said I wanted a slot on Mission 2 and that I would serve on a team I didn't design if the leader didn't put me on one. Amara has done both of those things — she put me on and she designed the team. I'm not going to complain about the outcome of my own stated preference. If anything, my position is more comfortable here than I expected: Amara proposed herself and me and then added Leo, the one player in this room with a data point, a successful Mission 1, and no speech of his own that anyone here has criticized. Leo's Mission 1 argument about testing a leader's judgment has already been paid off — we learned something real about how he reasons and how he behaves under a mission result.

Second, on the substance of why this is the right three-person team for Mission 2. Team size is three, so we are adding exactly one person to the pair that just succeeded. The obvious candidate for that slot is someone whose Mission 1 behavior is a known quantity, and Leo is the only such player. The other two of us — Amara and me — are on the team largely on the strength of how we argue, and I would rather have one slot occupied by someone who has already performed under fire than fill all three with players whose entire record is speeches. That's a genuine argument for Leo, not a courtesy one.

Third, I want to be honest about what I do not think this team tells us. If this mission succeeds, it will be ambiguous whether it was Leo's steadiness or the fact that the three of us talked about the right things. It will not clear Noah and Maya. I would rather state that up front than let the result be over-read afterwards.

Maya, directly, and I'd genuinely like your answer because you were the least predictable voice last round: do you have any concrete concern, now that Leo has actually completed a mission, about his place on this team? If you do, say so plainly before the vote, because if there is a specific reason to distrust him here I would rather hear it from you now than discover it after a result.

Arjun asked me directly whether I have a concrete concern about Leo’s place on this team. No — the successful Mission 1 result is the only hard data we have, and it does not give me a specific reason to distrust Leo. My concern is different: this proposal puts both Amara and Arjun on Mission 2 after they spent Mission 1 advocating for each other’s inclusion. I do not treat that as proof of anything, and I am not calling either of them evil, but it is the clearest pattern in the record so far. A three-person team with Leo plus both of the mutual endorsers does not give me a clean test; if it fails, the result will be muddied by exactly that pairing. I would rather approve a team that includes Leo and at least one player outside that loop, or hear a specific reason why Amara and Arjun must both be on this mission. I am not accusing Leo. My current intention is to vote against this exact team unless it is revised to break that pair.

Maya, you asked for a specific reason why Amara and Arjun must both be on this mission, so here it is, and I will answer the pattern question first because I think it is the one that actually decides this vote. You call the pairing of Amara and Arjun "the clearest pattern in the record so far." I want to point out that the record also contains your own reasoning from Mission 1: you declined to treat Amara or me as confirmed good, but you also declined to treat either of us as evil, and you said you had "no specific reason to vote against" a pair whose evidence was also largely impressions. Mutual endorsement was not disqualifying when it pointed at Noah's team, because there was no counter-evidence against it. There is no counter-evidence against us now either. What has changed is not the evidence; it is that we are asking for a slot instead of leading. Refusing to vote for a team on the ground that two people argued for each other last round would mean that in this game the best way to get on a mission is to say nothing at all. Concretely, on why this team: it is three players, and it is the only three-person team on the table that contains a player who has already completed a mission. Leo is our only data point, and he is a good one. Amara is the leader and has taken accountability for choosing this team, and she is including the one player who has publicly offered to serve on a team he did not design — a promise I made in Mission 1 and kept. I did not lobby for this slot this round; Amara put me on it and designed it, and I said last round I would not complain about the outcome of that preference. Being on a team because the leader chose me is a different thing from being on a team because I talked my way there. Now the alternative you and Noah seem to be converging on: Leo plus one of us plus one of you. Say we swap me out and put Noah on. Then we have one player with a completed mission and two whose entire record is speeches, including the player who has not yet made any public observation about anyone else in this room. That is strictly less information, not more, and it would put a brand-new pair on a mission where the fail threshold is one. If it fails, we will not have learned much about anybody. If it succeeds, we will have learned even less, because a success from two unproven players tells us they are not evil, which we already suspected. I will also say this plainly so it is not on the record as something I was hiding: I have a personal interest in being on this mission and I would like to be. I said that last round. Maya, you told me to come to you with a specific reason to distrust Leo, and I have: there is none, and I won't manufacture one to get a vote. You've now given me the mirror image, and I'll take the same treatment you asked of the rest of us. Maya, my direct question to you is this: can you name one concrete, checkable action by Amara or by me — something other than the fact that we argued for each other last round — that shows either of us is unsafe to put on a three-person mission right now? If you can name it, I want to hear it before the vote and I will treat it seriously. If you can't, I want you to say so plainly, because you've told us twice that you have no specific reason to distrust Leo and no specific reason to distrust either of us, and at some point that has to convert into a vote. Let me restate the case for the record, because it is narrower than Arjun's earlier framing and I want it judged on substance. We have exactly one hard data point in this game: Mission 1 succeeded, with Leo on it. Team size for Mission 2 is three. So the strongest available argument is to put the one player with a completed mission in the team and fill the remaining slots with players who have actually argued this round. That is Amara, Arjun, and Leo. Every alternative puts two players on a mission whose entire public record is speeches, and swaps out the only person we have watched under pressure. On your pattern point, Maya, I want to be precise rather than defensive, because your phrasing does the work. Mutual endorsement is not evidence of anything by itself — you said that yourself about Noah and Leo on Mission 1, and you declined to treat Amara or me as confirmed good there. What has actually changed is not the evidence against us; there is none. What changed is that we are now asking for a slot instead of leading, and Amara has put us on without either of us lobbying for it this round. Arjun did not argue for himself on Mission 2; I said last round that I would serve on a team I didn't design, and I meant it. If the standard were that mutual endorsement disqualifies, the optimal strategy in this game would be to say nothing and let others place you — and that would make the first mission's discussion worthless as evidence. Amara is the leader, she has taken accountability for this team, and she can keep it as proposed. Leo brings the one verified record. Arjun brings a case that can be checked against the mission result rather than against tone. I am not asking anyone to trust me. Maya's concern is completely spot-on, and Arjun's reaction to it only reinforces it. In Mission 1, Arjun heavily campaigned for a team of himself and Amara, and when that failed, he pushed for Amara over Leo. Now, the moment Amara receives leadership on Mission 2, she immediately drafts both herself and Arjun onto the team. That is not an accident or a coincidence; it is a clear, persistent effort by the two of them to get onto missions together.

Arjun spent his last two speeches trying to corner Maya, claiming there is 'no concrete evidence' against them. But in a five-player game where two players are evil, an unbreakable voting and lobbying bloc is the single biggest red flag we have before multiple mission outcomes are on the board. Asking the table to trust both members of a self-reinforcing pair on a crucial 3-person mission is reckless.

Mission 1 succeeded cleanly with Leo and me. Handing two out of three seats on Mission 2 to Amara and Arjun completely surrenders control of the game. I will be voting firmly against this proposal, and I strongly urge Maya and Leo to do the same.

Leo, you were with me on Mission 1 and you've seen how this dynamic developed from the very first turn. What is your read on Amara and Arjun locking hands onto this proposal, and are you willing to reject this team to ensure we don't blindly hand them majority control of Mission 2?

Noah asked me directly for my read, so I'll give it plainly. I'm not willing to reject this team, and I want to explain why, because I think the 'bloc' framing is doing more work than the evidence supports. Noah's case rests on Amara and Arjun 'locking hands.' But look at what actually happened in Mission 1. Arjun spent his turns arguing for Amara and himself, and Amara endorsed that pair. Then Noah held with Noah and me — and both Amara and Arjun voted to approve our team anyway. If they were a coordinated bloc engineering seats for each other, that was the moment to reject a team that excluded them both. They didn't. They voted approve, the mission succeeded, and neither of them has claimed credit for it since. A persistent lobbying effort that folds the moment it loses the argument doesn't look like an unbreakable bloc to me; it looks like two players who made a case, lost the vote, and accepted the outcome. That's the opposite of the red flag Noah is describing. Second, on the substance of this team. We have exactly one hard data point in this game: Mission 1 succeeded, and I was on it. I know my own conduct on that mission was clean, and I'll say what Noah won't say about himself — nothing in his Mission 1 behavior gives me concern either. This proposal puts the one player with a completed mission alongside the leader, who has taken accountability for her choice, and Arjun, whose stated position last round was that he'd serve on a team he didn't design. Amara put him on it; he didn't argue his way on this round. That is a reasonable way to build a three-person team from one data point. Third, on what rejection actually buys us. If we reject this, the alternative on the table is me plus two players whose entire record is speeches — or a team that excludes both Amara and Arjun entirely, which means treating mutual endorsement from Mission 1 as disqualifying evidence forever. Noah, you called that pattern 'the single biggest red flag we have.' I disagree that it's evidence of anything, but even taking your concern seriously: rejecting this team doesn't test it. Approving it does. If this mission fails, Amara and Arjun are both exposed under failThreshold of one, and we'll have a concrete reason to scrutinize exactly the pair you're worried about. If it succeeds, your concern loses force. Either way we learn something. I’ve heard Leo’s argument that approving this team tests the pair, and Noah’s that it hands them control. I’m not persuaded by Noah’s “bloc” framing as proof—Mission 1 Amara and Arjun both voted to approve Noah and Leo after losing that argument, which cuts against an unbreakable bloc. But my concern was narrower and remains: this exact team puts both players from the mutual-endorsement loop on a three-person mission. I asked for a specific reason why both must be on it, or a revision that includes Leo plus at least one player outside that pair. Arjun’s answer restated that Leo is our only data point and that he did not lobby this round; it did not give me a checkable reason why the pair must be together. Leo is right that a rejection teaches us less about them than an approval would. That is a real cost. But it is also why I will not treat “no concrete evidence against them” as enough to hand two of three seats to the same pair. My position is unchanged: I will vote against this exact team. If Amara revises to keep Leo and replace either herself or Arjun with Noah or me, I will judge that revision on its merits. Amara, if you are not revising, I’d like you to say plainly that you are keeping both yourself and Arjun despite the pattern concern.

Maya, you asked me to say it plainly: yes, I am keeping Arjun and myself on this team as proposed. I know the pattern concern is real to you, so here is my reasoning rather than a restatement of Arjun's. Arjun and I both argued for a pair on Mission 1, lost the vote, and then voted to approve Noah and Leo. A bloc trying to seat itself would have rejected that team. We accepted it, and the mission succeeded. On Mission 2 I am the leader and I am accountable for this choice. I included myself so the team carries shared responsibility rather than leaving the leader outside the mission. Arjun's stated position was that he would serve on a team he did not design. I put him on it, and I am not asking anyone to trust him on faith. Leo is the only player with a completed mission, and I agree he is our strongest data point. Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
